name: webpack

foundation.via: A founding project, from the JS Foundation it joined in 2016

summary: The JavaScript bundler built around code splitting, loaders and plugins: written in JavaScript, highly configurable, and still downloaded tens of millions of times a week.
intro: webpack is a static module bundler. Starting from one or more entry points, it follows every `import` and `require` to build a dependency graph, then writes the modules into one or more bundles to serve. Out of the box it understands JavaScript, JSON and WebAssembly. Anything else goes through loaders, functions that turn a file into modules (`babel-loader` for modern syntax, `ts-loader` for TypeScript), while plugins hook into the whole compilation for jobs such as minifying, injecting environment variables or writing HTML. Since webpack 4 a config file is optional: it bundles `./src/index.js` into `./dist/main.js`, and `mode` switches between development and production defaults.

webpack 5, released on October 10, 2020, is still the current major; version 5.112 came out in October 2026. It added an opt-in persistent file-system cache, asset modules, and Module Federation, which lets separately built and deployed apps load modules from each other at run time. It also stopped polyfilling Node.js core modules for the browser. The 2026 roadmap moves common plugins into the core: native CSS and HTML entry points as `experiments` options, TypeScript `tsconfig` paths (shipped in 5.105) and, later, TypeScript without a loader, ahead of a webpack 6 that has no release date.

Its position has changed. Faster tools have taken over new projects: Vite, which builds with Rolldown since Vite 8, now has more than three times webpack’s npm downloads, and Next.js 16 (October 2025) made Turbopack its default and kept webpack behind a `--webpack` flag. ByteDance’s Rspack, written in Rust, implements webpack’s API and runs most of its loaders and plugins, as a faster drop-in replacement. webpack itself is maintained mostly by volunteers. In the week to October 27, 2026 it was still downloaded about 63 million times from npm, against about 212 million for Vite.
strengths: Fine control over output: code splitting at every dynamic `import()`, `splitChunks` rules for shared code, and content-hashed file names for long-term caching
Module Federation for loading code from separately deployed builds at run time
A huge ecosystem of loaders and plugins, and a stable API that Rspack also implements, so large existing setups keep working
Persistent caching makes rebuilds of large projects much faster after the first one
limits: Written in JavaScript: cold builds and dev-server start-up are slower than Rust and Go bundlers such as Rspack, Rolldown and esbuild
Configuration grows quickly; loaders, plugins and their interactions are a common source of hard-to-debug builds
The dev server bundles the app before serving it, unlike Vite, which serves source modules on demand
Volunteer-maintained with no full-time team, and frameworks such as Next.js have moved their defaults to other bundlers

snippet.title: A production config with caching, a split vendor chunk and native CSS
source: filename: '[name].[contenthash].js',   // new hash only when the content changes
rules: [{ test: /\.ts$/, use: 'ts-loader' }],   // loaders turn other files into modules
experiments: { css: true },   // import './app.css' without css-loader or plugins
cache: { type: 'filesystem' },   // reuse work between builds
splitChunks: { chunks: 'all' },   // node_modules code goes into its own chunk
// every dynamic import('./chart.ts') in the source also becomes its own chunk

story: Tobias Koppers came to JavaScript from Java, where Google Web Toolkit could split an application into pieces loaded on demand. He missed that in JavaScript tooling, proposed it to the modules-webmake bundler, and when the change did not go forward wrote his own bundler in 2012. Instagram’s front-end team found an early version and adopted it, partly for code splitting, and Pete Hunt’s talk about it at OSCON in 2014 brought it a wide audience.

webpack 1.0 came out in February 2014. It followed imports itself, used loaders to bring CSS, images and other files into the same dependency graph, and split code at chosen points. webpack 4 (February 2018) introduced `mode` and made configuration optional, and webpack 5 (October 2020) added persistent caching and Module Federation. The project joined the JS Foundation at its launch on October 17, 2016, and became part of the OpenJS Foundation when that merged with the Node.js Foundation in March 2019.

In the 2020s faster tools written in Go and Rust took over new projects; Koppers himself is on the team behind Turbopack, which Next.js 16 made its default bundler in October 2025. webpack’s 2026 roadmap, from its technical steering committee, aims to keep it a “stable and well-supported choice” by folding common plugins into the core and preparing webpack 6, while asking for donations to pay its volunteer contributors.

choices.why: Koppers wanted GWT’s ability to load parts of an app on demand. Building bundles around split points let large apps such as Instagram load only the code a page needs.

choices.choice: Everything is a module, through loaders
choices.why: Treating CSS, images and other files as modules that loaders transform let one dependency graph cover the whole front end, instead of separate pipelines per file type.

Every project had to write a config file, even when it needed nothing beyond an entry and an output. Defaults for those, plus a production or development `mode` that turns on the matching optimisations, let small projects start without one.

choices.choice: Move common plugins into the core (2026 roadmap)
choices.why: CSS extraction, HTML generation and TypeScript each needed a separate plugin or loader. Building them in reduces dependencies and gives a volunteer team fewer packages to maintain.
